question: How do they identify discussions of LGBTQ people in the New York Times?

extractive_spans: act paragraphs containing any word from a predetermined list of LGTBQ terms
evidence: The data for our case study spans over thirty years of articles from the New York Times, from January 1986 to December 2015, and was originally collected by BIBREF68 BIBREF68. The articles come from all sections of the newspaper, such as “World", “New York & Region", “Opinion", “Style", and “Sports". Our distributional semantic methods rely on all of the available data in order to obtain the most fine-grained understanding of the relationships between words possible. For the other techniques, we extract paragraphs containing any word from a predetermined list of LGTBQ terms (shown in Table TABREF19).

title: A Framework for the Computational Linguistic Analysis of Dehumanization
answer_short: By analyzing linguistic cues, particularly comparing 'gay' and 'homosexual' against the control label 'American(s)' to detect dehumanizing language trends over time.
answer_rationale: The study identifies LGBTQ discussions in the New York Times by comparing linguistic patterns of 'gay' and 'homosexual' against the control label 'American(s)' to detect dehumanizing language trends over time. This method is explicitly described in the retrieved documents, particularly in Text 1 (source_id=65), which explains the rationale for using 'American(s)' as a control variable to contrast changes in LGBTQ label representation. Text 4 (source_id=2) further supports this by stating the framework applies to analyzing discussions of LGBTQ people in the New York Times using linguistic correlates of dehumanization. Text 3 (source_id=132) confirms the focus on 'gay' and 'homosexual' due to data availability, reinforcing the methodological approach.
